MUJAHID:v1p231#2/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p231#2/r1.speaker: عبيد بن عمير الليثي
MUJAHID:v1p231#2/r1.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr al-Laythi says that a huge, tall, gluttonous drinker will weigh no more than a mosquito's wing with God.

MUQATIL:7:7-9/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:7:7-9/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:7:7-9/r2.claim: The weighing of deeds is justice; believers succeed if even an atom's weight tips their good deeds over their sins.

TAB-FULL:v10p68/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r1.claim: الوزن is the verbal noun of وزن, with forms وزنا and وزنة; in the verse it means the just weighing on the Day people are questioned.

TAB-FULL:v10p68/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r2.claim: Mujahid glosses الوزن as judgment or adjudication and understands الحق as justice.

TAB-FULL:v10p68/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r3.claim: Mujahid separately glosses الحق as justice.

TAB-FULL:v10p68/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r4.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r4.claim: Al-Suddi says that deeds themselves are weighed.

TAB-FULL:v10p68/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r5.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r5.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says a huge, tall, heavily eating and drinking man will weigh no more than a mosquito’s wing.

TAB-FULL:v10p68/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r6.speaker: حذيفة
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r6.claim: Hudhayfa says Gabriel oversees the scales and restores rights to the wronged; if needed, the wrongdoer bears another’s sins and returns with a mountain-like burden.

TAB-FULL:v10p68/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r7.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r7.claim: Mujahid interprets heavy scales as abundant good deeds.

TAB-FULL:v10p68/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r8.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
TAB-FULL:v10p68/r8.claim: Another view takes the scales literally as the familiar balance with a tongue and two pans, used to weigh good and bad deeds.

TAB-FULL:v10p70/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p70/r1.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
TAB-FULL:v10p70/r1.claim: Amr ibn Dinar says the Judgment balance is a familiar scale with two pans.

TAB-FULL:v10p70/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p70/r2.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
TAB-FULL:v10p70/r2.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says a tall, huge man is placed on the scale yet does not weigh a fly’s wing.

TAB-FULL:v10p70/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p70/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v10p70/r3.claim: Al-Tabari prefers the ordinary balance interpretation: God weighs good and bad deeds, as Prophetic reports about good character being weightiest confirm.

TAB-FULL:v10p70/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p70/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v10p70/r4.claim: Although God already knows the measure of deeds and deeds are not bodies, weighing them is like recording them: it provides evidence for or against people according to their obedience, without need or fear of forgetfulness.

TAB-FULL:v10p71/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p71/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
TAB-FULL:v10p71/r1.claim: Ibn Amr reports that a man’s ninety-nine sin-records are outweighed by a tiny record testifying that there is no god but God and Muhammad is His servant and messenger.

TAB-FULL:v10p71/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p71/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v10p71/r2.claim: God weighs people by placing the person and records of good deeds in one pan, and records of bad deeds in the other; He creates the appropriate heaviness or lightness as evidence, like making limbs testify.

TAB-FULL:v10p71/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v10p71/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v10p71/r3.claim: Al-Tabari rejects denial of the familiar balance: revelation and Prophetic reports affirm heavy and light scales, while neither reason nor transmitted proof rules this interpretation out.

ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r1.speaker: قال بعضهم
ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r1.claim: Some say the resurrection scale has two pans and was sent down for people to transact justly and weigh deeds.

ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r2.speaker: قال بعضهم
ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r2.claim: Others interpret the scale as justice, using weighing metaphorically for what is equivalent in the mind.

ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r3.speaker: قال بعضهم
ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r3.claim: Another view identifies the scale with the record book of human deeds.

ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r4.claim: All are linguistically possible, but the author says to follow sound transmitted reports; if reliable transmission says it has two pans, that should be accepted.

ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r5.speaker: الضحاك
ZAJJAJ:v2p319/r5.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, in a report from Jarīr, says the scale is justice.

IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r1.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r1.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says a very tall, large eater and drinker may still weigh no more than a mosquito's wing.

IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r2.claim: Mujahid glosses the weighing as justice.

IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r3.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r3.claim: Al-Suddi says the weighing refers to deeds.

IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r4.claim: Mujahid also glosses the weighing as judgment.

IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r5.claim: Mujahid says those whose scales are heavy are those whose good deeds are heavy.

IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v5p1440#2/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says the successful have attained what they sought and escaped what they feared.

SULAMI:v1p220#5/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p220#5/r1.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p220#5/r1.claim: Weighing oneself by justice marks a humble person; weighing thoughts and breaths by truth leaves one content with divine witnessing.

SULAMI:v1p220#5/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p220#5/r2.speaker: author
SULAMI:v1p220#5/r2.claim: The soul-and-spirit scale weighs obedience and disobedience by the Book and Sunna; the heart-and-intellect scale weighs reward and punishment by promise and warning.

SULAMI:v1p220#5/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p220#5/r3.speaker: author
SULAMI:v1p220#5/r3.claim: The gnosis-and-secret scale weighs approval and displeasure, with flight and seeking as its two pans.

THALABI:v4p216/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p216/r1.claim: Weighing deeds tests faith in worldly life, marks the saved and doomed in the next, shows people their recompense, and establishes the proof against them.

THALABI:v4p216/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p216/r2.claim: The weighing is comparable to the record that speaks with truth and sets out people’s deeds, despite God already knowing them.

THALABI:v4p216/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r3.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v4p216/r3.claim: Mujahid identifies the heavy balance-pan with a person’s good deeds.

THALABI:v4p216/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r5.speaker: حذيفة
THALABI:v4p216/r5.claim: Gabriel weighs people’s deeds; wrongdoers’ good deeds transfer to victims, or victims’ sins are loaded onto them, leaving them burdened like mountains.

THALABI:v4p216/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v4p216/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas describes a balance with tongue and two pans: a believer’s beautiful deeds outweigh sins and lead to Paradise, while a disbeliever’s ugly deeds are light and fall into Hell.

THALABI:v4p216/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p216/r7.claim: Since deeds are accidents, the weighed objects are written records containing people’s deeds.

THALABI:v4p216/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r8.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
THALABI:v4p216/r8.claim: A man’s ninety-nine enormous sin-records are outweighed by a tiny card bearing the testimony that there is no deity but God and Muhammad is His messenger.

THALABI:v4p216/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p216/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p216/r9.claim: The weighing is linked to the promise that just balances will be set up for the Day of Resurrection.

THALABI:v4p217/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p217/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p217/r1.claim: The plural mawazin may be a plural form with singular meaning, like plural terms in the cited verse and al-Aʿsha’s poetry.

THALABI:v4p217/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p217/r2.speaker: الأعشى
THALABI:v4p217/r2.claim: Al-Aʿsha’s line uses plural ‘breasts’ and ‘forearms’ while intending one of each.

THALABI:v4p217/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p217/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p217/r3.claim: Other interpretations take the plural as the deeds being weighed, or as one great balance with a balance for each servant.

THALABI:v4p217/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p217/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p217/r4.claim: The plural can refer to the whole balance assembly: its two pans, beam, and tongue, which must come together for weighing.

THALABI:v4p217/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v4p217/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v4p217/r5.claim: A moral interpretation calls reason the balance distinguishing truth from falsehood, knowledge the balance distinguishing lawful from unlawful, and sound will the balance distinguishing felicity from misery.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r1.claim: Mujahid interprets the true weighing as judgment according to justice; another view says good and bad deeds are weighed through signs people see on Judgment Day.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r2.speaker: الحسن
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r2.claim: Al-Hasan and others affirm a real scale with two pans for weighing good and bad deeds.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r3.speaker: الحسن
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r3.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Suddi say the deeds themselves are weighed, with good and bad placed in opposite pans.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r4.claim: Abdullah ibn Umar says the records of deeds are weighed, since good and bad actions are acts while weighing applies to bodies.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r5.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r5.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says people themselves are weighed; a huge man may weigh less than a mosquito's wing.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r6.claim: A heavy scale may mean a person judged to have obeyed, or whose good deeds outweigh bad deeds, or whose good deeds simply exceed them.

MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v2p201/r7.claim: The successful are those rewarded for their good deeds; the opposite applies when the scales are light.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says those made successful are saved, as in the verse about setting just scales on the Day of Resurrection.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r2.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r2.claim: Muqatil calls the weighing justice and says a believer succeeds when even an atom's weight outweighs his sins.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r3.claim: The source gives two accounts of how deeds are weighed: deeds assume beautiful or ugly forms, or the written records of deeds are weighed; the Prophet reportedly answered that records are weighed.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r4.claim: Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-Aʿmash interpret weighing and scales as justice and judgment, figurative expressions rather than literal weighing.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r5.claim: A poet uses 'my scale for every disputant' to mean words equal to an opponent's; figuratively, scales can denote justice and records that accurately report deeds.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r6.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r6.claim: Abu Ishaq says the figurative argument is linguistically valid, but authentic reports mentioning a scale should take precedence.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r7.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24#2/r7.claim: Ibn al-Anbari chooses literal weighing because reports converge, most scholars agree, and the Quran's surface supports it; the plural can reflect generic من or a plural referent.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24/r1.claim: The weighing is on the day of questioning; al-wazn is the subject and al-haqq its predicate, and Ibn Abbas with most exegetes takes it as weighing people's deeds.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24/r2.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24/r2.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says the scales establish the case against people, remove their excuses, and make God's justice clear.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p24/r3.claim: A report says God will set up a scale with a tongue and two pans to weigh people's good and evil deeds.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p26/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p26/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v9p26/r1.claim: Another grammarian says mawāzīn means things weighed, not multiple scales; it refers to weighed deeds.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:5-8/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:5-8/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:5-8/r4.claim: The weighing occurs on the day of questioning; believers' deeds appear as beautiful forms and unbelievers' deeds as ugly forms, which are weighed.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:5-8/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:5-8/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:7:5-8/r5.claim: Those whose scales are heavy are believers who escape and succeed.

JISHUMI:v4p2499/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r11.speaker: الفراء
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r11.claim: In يومئذ الحق, الحق may be nominative as the predicate of الوزن or accusative as a verbal noun, with يومئذ as predicate.

JISHUMI:v4p2499/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r3.claim: Weighing compares two things to reveal their relative measure, then extends metaphorically to prosody and measured speech; thaqal is opposite lightness.

JISHUMI:v4p2499/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r4.speaker: أبو هاشم
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r4.claim: Abū Hāshim treats heaviness as a distinct attribute in a heavy object: a necessary downward tendency.

JISHUMI:v4p2499/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r5.speaker: أبو علي
JISHUMI:v4p2499/r5.claim: Abū ʿAlī says heaviness reduces to the parts composing the heavy object; they agree that lightness is no positive attribute but the absence of heaviness.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r3.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r3.claim: Mujahid interprets the weighing on that day as just judgment.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r4.speaker: أكثرون
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r4.claim: Most interpreters understand this as the weighing of deeds on a real balance with a tongue and two pans spanning the distance between east and west.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r5.claim: One view weighs written records; a man’s ninety-nine scrolls are outweighed by a card bearing the testimony of faith.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r6.claim: Another view weighs people themselves; the Prophet says a huge, heavy man may weigh less before God than a mosquito’s wing.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that deeds are weighed after being embodied as beautiful forms for good deeds and ugly forms for bad deeds.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r8.claim: The weighing tests people’s faith, which they held in worldly life, and establishes proof against them in the next life.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r9.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v3p214#2/r9.claim: Mujahid identifies the heavy scales with a person’s good deeds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r1.claim: Al-wazn is a verbal noun; the verse can be parsed with 'the weight' as subject and 'the truth' as predicate, or 'that day' as predicate and 'true' as an adjective: true weighing is established or manifest on Judgment Day.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r2.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r2.claim: One group takes scales and weighing as a metaphor for the meticulous justice of Judgment, using the familiar image of a balance; Abu Talib's verse illustrates this sense.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r3.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the metaphorical view is weaker: Qur'anic wording and a Prophetic report direct a person to seek the Prophet at the visible balance, weighing poses no problem, and abandoning the literal sense without cause risks denying revealed realities.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r4.speaker: مجاهد، الضحاك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r4.claim: This metaphorical view is also reported from Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and others, who understand heaviness and lightness as the abundance or scarcity of good deeds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r5.speaker: جمهور الأمة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r5.claim: The majority say the Judgment balance has a beam and two pans like worldly balances, displaying exact justice through a familiar object.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r6.speaker: حذيفة بن اليمان
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p375/r6.claim: Hudhayfa says Gabriel is the custodian of the balances on Judgment Day.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r1.claim: The balance should be understood literally; reports say records of good and bad deeds go into its pans, where God creates heaviness or lightness.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r2.claim: Weight must occur in a body, since an accident cannot inhere in another accident; it may occur in the records or nearby bodies, and Abu al-Maali favors the records.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r3.claim: Unreliable reports about the balance's shape and length need not be repeated; Hasan's report that each person has a separate balance is rejected because the balance is one, though each person has an individual weighing.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r4.speaker: مجاهد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r4.claim: Mujahid says the 'scales' are the good deeds themselves; Ibn Atiyya says the plural highlights the many weighed acts.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r5.claim: Mufliḥūn are those who attain what they seek and succeed; the cited poem uses aflaḥa for attainment, while another verse may use falāḥ for survival, which is closely related.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r6.claim: God's weighing, recording deeds, and making limbs testify despite His knowledge serve to establish proof; the testimony of divine oneness must tip a person's balance.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p376/r7.claim: The author asks how sinful believers can have a weighty balance and be judged successful yet still enter Hell.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r3.speaker: طائفة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r3.claim: One answer is that good deeds are weighed without tawhid first, then tawhid makes the balance heavy when sinful believers are released from Hell.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r4.claim: Knowing that a sinner will not remain forever in Hell counts as success, even if disciplinary punishment comes first.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r5.speaker: طائفة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r5.claim: One answer is that good deeds are weighed without tawhid first, then tawhid makes the balance heavy when sinful believers are released from Hell.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p377/r6.claim: Knowing that a sinner will not remain forever in Hell counts as success, even if disciplinary punishment comes first.

TABRISI:7:6-9/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:6-9/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:7:6-9/r2.claim: Mīzān means comparing two things to reveal their measure and extends metaphorically to poetic meter and measured speech; truth is putting things where wisdom requires, while weight is downward force and lightness upward force.

TABRISI:7:7-8/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:7-8/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:7:7-8/r10.claim: The author prefers the metaphorical justice reading, followed by the literal scale, since Arabs call apt words and deeds “weighed”; he also considers the literal view supported by transmitted reports and the apparent wording.

TABRISI:7:7-8/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:7-8/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TABRISI:7:7-8/r3.claim: Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Balkhī understand the balance as justice in the afterlife, where no one is wronged.

TABRISI:7:7-8/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:7-8/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:7:7-8/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and al-Jubbāʾī say God sets up a real balance with a tongue and two pans to weigh good and bad deeds.

TABRISI:7:7-8/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:7-8/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
TABRISI:7:7-8/r5.claim: One proposed account is that the records of deeds themselves are weighed, reported from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar and others.

TABRISI:7:7-8/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:7-8/r6.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:7:7-8/r6.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī offers the possibility that signs of good and bad deeds appear in the balance's pans and are seen by people.

TABRISI:7:7-8/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:7-8/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:7:7-8/r7.claim: Another view from Ibn ʿAbbās says good deeds are shown in a beautiful form and bad deeds in an ugly form.

TABRISI:7:7-8/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:7-8/r8.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
TABRISI:7:7-8/r8.claim: ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr says the believer and unbeliever themselves are weighed; a physically huge man may weigh less than a gnat's wing.

TABRISI:7:7-8/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:7-8/r9.speaker: أبو مسلم
TABRISI:7:7-8/r9.claim: Abū Muslim reads weighing as the believer's high standing and the unbeliever's humiliation, like the declaration that they will have no weight in 18:105.

TABRISI:7:8-9/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:8-9/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:7:8-9/r1.claim: The poetic example speaks of measured, sound speech, including indirect expression; weighing may mean that something stands in the mind as equal to its comparison.

TABRISI:7:8-9/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:8-9/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:7:8-9/r2.claim: Mawāzīn is plural because each kind of worship may have its own scale, or each scale may correspond to a category of a person's deeds; a report says prayer is a scale.

TABRISI:7:8-9/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:7:8-9/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:7:8-9/r3.claim: Those whose scales are heavy succeed by winning God's reward.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r1.claim: God will report to the messengers and nations what they did, knowing it and never being absent from them.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#2/r2.claim: The record will be placed and will speak of what people used to do.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#3/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v3p169#3/r1.claim: The weight is justice; the plural “scales” treats the generic person collectively, as the following plural pronoun confirms.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r1.claim: The weighing follows the questioning and accounting described earlier; the phrase can be parsed with يومئذ as an adverb and الحق as predicate, or as predicate with الحق describing a just weighing.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r2.claim: One literal view says God sets up a balance with a pointer and two pans; Ibn Abbas says the believer's deeds appear in their best form and good deeds outweigh evil, as in 21:47.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says a believer's deeds are transformed into a beautiful image for weighing, while most exegetes instead say the weighed items are the written records; a prophetic answer to what is weighed is reported as the records.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن سلام
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r4.claim: Ibn Salam describes a balance between jinn and humans facing the Throne, with one pan toward Paradise and one toward Hell, large enough to hold the heavens and earth, watched by Gabriel.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r5.claim: Ibn Umar reports a man whose 99 scrolls of sins, each as long as sight, are outweighed by a tiny card bearing the testimony that none is god but God and Muhammad is His messenger.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r6.speaker: الحسن
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r6.claim: Hasan reports that when Aisha asked about people remembering one another at resurrection, the Prophet said they would be barefoot and unclothed and too occupied with records and weighing to remember anyone, citing 80:37.

RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r7.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
RAZI-FULL:v14p21#2/r7.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr says a huge, voracious drinker may have no weight even equal to a gnat.

RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r1.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك والأعمش
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r1.claim: Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-A'mash, followed by many later scholars, take the balance as justice and judgment rather than a literal scale.

RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r2.claim: Supporters of the figurative reading say weight can mean justice because worldly fairness in taking and giving is shown by weights; Arabic also uses weight figuratively for worth and equality, as in 18:105.

RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r3.claim: A poem cited by the author uses ميزانه for the balance of an opponent's argument: the speaker had a measure for every disputant, meaning a reply of equal force, not a physical scale.

RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r4.claim: Razi insists the verse must mean only justice: deeds are transient accidents, so cannot be weighed; even if they persisted, weighing is useless because believers already know God's justice and others could suspect a staged result.

RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r5.speaker: أصحاب القول الأول
RAZI-FULL:v14p22/r5.claim: Literal-scale proponents answer that everyone knows God is just and the scale publicly displays the result: a favorable balance increases joy, an unfavorable one increases grief and shame; some describe light or darkness, others a tilted pan.

RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r1.claim: Razi finds several actual balances more apparent than one, citing 21:47 and the verse's plural; separate balances may measure heart, bodily, and spoken acts.

RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r2.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r2.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains the plural either as Arabic using a plural for one object or as referring to the things weighed, meaning deeds rather than balances; Razi says both abandon the plain plural despite no obstacle to multiple scales.

RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r3.claim: The heavy and light balances divide humanity into two groups: those whose good deeds exceed their bad and those whose bad exceed their good; no group has equal totals.

RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r4.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r4.claim: Most exegetes identify those whose balances are light as unbelievers, because being described as wronging God's signs means denying them.

RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r5.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v14p23/r5.claim: Al-Wahidi's al-Basit reports that the Prophet's prayer-card can outweigh a believer's weak good deeds; the wider scholarly report instead gives the card bearing the testimony of faith, which al-Qadi says must be paired with its obligations to avoid encouraging sin.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r1.speaker: ابن عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r1.claim: The Prophet says God draws a believer close, makes him acknowledge his sins, then forgives him and gives him his record of good deeds; disbelievers and hypocrites are publicly exposed.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r2.claim: The believer’s delivery of a record of good deeds proves deeds are written in records and weighed.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r3.claim: A hadith describes a man’s ninety-nine vast records outweighed by a small card affirming God’s oneness and Muhammad’s messengership; al-Tirmidhi adds that nothing outweighs God’s name and grades it hasan gharib.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r4.claim: The plural ‘balances’ may mean multiple scales, one for each class of deed, or a single balance expressed in the plural, like travel by ships or mules.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#2/r5.claim: Another grammatical interpretation takes ‘balances’ as the plural of weighed things, meaning the deeds being weighed rather than the scales themselves.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#3/r1.speaker: القشيري
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#3/r1.claim: Al-Qushayri reports that the Prophet places a small card in the balance when a believer’s good deeds are light; it bears the reward of the believer’s prayers for the Prophet, repaid when most needed.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#3/r2.speaker: القشيري
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#3/r2.claim: Al-Qushayri explains that bitāqa, with kasra on its first letter, means a small slip recording goods in Egyptian usage.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#3/r3.speaker: محمد بن يحيى
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9#3/r3.claim: Ibn Majah’s Muhammad ibn Yahya likewise says bitāqa means a slip of paper, as Egyptians call a slip.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r1.claim: ‘The weighing that day is true’ can be parsed as subject and predicate, with ‘true’ as an adjective, or with ‘true’ as an accusative verbal noun.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r10.claim: Qurtubi’s preferred account is that deeds written in records are placed in the balance’s pans, as the report of the shahada card demonstrates.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r11.speaker: صفوان بن محرز
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r11.claim: A Sahih Muslim narration from Safwan preserves Ibn Umar’s report of the Prophet’s conversation with God about the believer’s record.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r2.claim: The verse means deeds are weighed on the balance; Ibn Umar says the records of people’s deeds are weighed, which Qurtubi calls correct based on transmitted reports.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r3.claim: Another view says the balance is the book in which people’s deeds are written.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r4.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r4.claim: Mujahid says the good and evil deeds themselves are weighed.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r5.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك والأعمش
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r5.claim: Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-A‘mash take weighing and balance as metaphors for justice and judgment, as ordinary speech uses weight to mean equivalence.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r6.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r6.claim: Al-Zajjaj accepts the metaphor as linguistically sound, but Qurtubi prefers the sound reports affirming a real balance.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r7.speaker: القشيري
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r7.claim: Al-Qushayri argues that metaphorizing the balance would also invite metaphorizing the Path, Paradise and Fire, jinn, and angels; the early community accepted these descriptions literally.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r8.speaker: المعتزلة
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r8.claim: The Mu‘tazilites deny the balance because accidents cannot be weighed and do not subsist independently.

QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r9.speaker: بعض المتكلمين
QURTUBI-FULL:7:8-9/r9.claim: Some theologians say God turns accidents into bodies for weighing; Qurtubi rejects this and holds that written records make the scales heavier or lighter.

BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r1.claim: Al-wazn may mean judgment or the weighing of deeds by comparison with their recompense.

BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r2.claim: Most scholars hold that records of deeds are weighed on a balance with a tongue and two pans, publicly demonstrating justice and removing excuses, as people's deeds are also elicited and acknowledged by speech and limbs.

BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r3.claim: A report describes a man given ninety-nine scrolls, each as far as the eye can reach, and a card bearing the two testimonies; the card outweighs the scrolls.

BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r4.claim: Another view weighs people themselves, supported by the prophetic report that a huge, heavy man will weigh no more than a gnat's wing with God.

BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r5.claim: Al-haqq is either an adjective describing the weighing or the predicate of an omitted subject; it means just and sound.

BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:7:8/r6.claim: Heavy scales mean good deeds or what weighs them; the plural reflects differing weighed things or multiple weighings, and the successful are those saved and rewarded.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r1.claim: The weighing is the weighing and distinguishing of deeds by relative heaviness; يومئذ means the day God questions nations and messengers, with the clause omitted and replaced by nunation.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r2.claim: One view says records of deeds will be weighed on a scale with a tongue and two pans, manifesting the attribute and ending excuses; another takes the phrase as just judgment, while God knows its manner.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r3.claim: Mawāzīn can mean scales or weighed deeds; what has weight and worth is good deeds or the measure used for them.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p4#3/r4.claim: Those whose balances are heavy are the successful, meaning victorious.

QASHANI:7:8-9/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:7:8-9/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:7:8-9/r1.claim: Weighing is assessment of deeds at the lesser resurrection and is just or real; lasting good deeds weigh heavily and yield the heart's paradise of divine attributes.

QASHANI:7:8-9/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:7:8-9/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:7:8-9/r2.claim: The scale's tongue is justice, with sense and intellect as its pans; enduring rational acquisitions, virtues, good works, and sincere intentions have weight, unlike transient sensations, desires, and vices.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r10.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r10.claim: Hasan holds that every person has a separate balance on the Day of Resurrection.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r11.claim: Balances can also stand for good deeds by ellipsis: the balance-pan of a person’s weighed deeds becomes heavy or light.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r12.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r12.claim: Grammatically, weighing is the subject and the time expression supplies its predicate, with the sense that the weighing occurs when God questions people and recounts their deeds on Judgment Day.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r13.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r13.claim: The word true may qualify the weighing, or the time phrase may modify weighing and true may be its predicate.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r4.claim: Exegetes disagree whether the weighing is a real balance or a figure for complete justice, sound judgment, and exact reckoning.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r5.speaker: المعتزلة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r5.claim: The Muʿtazila, preceded in this view by Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-Aʿmash, deny a literal balance and take heaviness and lightness as abundance or scarcity of good deeds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r6.speaker: جمهور الأمة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r6.claim: The majority affirm a real balance with a shaft, two pans, and a tongue, shown to all creatures to establish proof, justice, and the end of excuses.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r7.claim: The visible balance confirms the judgment alongside questioning, people’s admissions, testimony by limbs, prophets, angels, and witnesses.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r8.claim: Reports say the weighed objects are the records on which deeds were written; God creates heaviness or lightness in them, while reports about the balance’s dimensions and form have unsound chains.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r9.speaker: جمهور الأمة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v5p13/r9.claim: The majority explain plural balances by the multiplicity of objects weighed, although there is one balance.

SAMIN-DURR:7:8#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:8#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:7:8#2/r1.claim: موازين may be the plural of ميزان, the instrument: one scale for each person according to exegetical reports, or scales corresponding to numerous deeds; the state is expressed through its place.

SAMIN-DURR:7:8#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:8#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:7:8#2/r2.claim: Alternatively, موازين is the plural of موزون and refers to the deeds being weighed.

SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r1.claim: On the first parse, الوزن is the subject and يومئذ is its predicate; the genitive clause after إذ is omitted and its tanwin compensates for it, as the majority hold against al-Akhfash.

SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r2.speaker: الجمهور
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r2.claim: The majority treat the tanwin in يومئذ as compensation for the omitted genitive clause after إذ; al-Akhfash disagrees.

SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r3.speaker: مكي
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r3.claim: If يومئذ is the predicate, الحق may be an adjective of الوزن, an omitted predicate answering what the weighing is, or—unusually—an appositive to the pronoun within the adverb.

SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r4.claim: An alternative makes الحق the predicate and يومئذ either a time adverb governed by الوزن or, very weakly, a broad object.

SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r5.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r5.claim: Abu al-Baqa rejects treating الحق as an adjective after يومئذ because he sees an interruption between the relative and its clause.

SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r6.claim: The relative clause is already complete before الحق, so the adjective is not separated from its clause; that adjective parse would instead leave the subject without a predicate.

SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:7:8/r7.claim: Detailed hypothetical rearrangements of الحق and يومئذ, and discussion of an unattested accusative reading, are unnecessary because the Qur'an's wording is fixed.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r1.claim: One view weighs deeds themselves, which God turns into bodies; al-Baghawi reports this from Ibn Abbas, with traditions portraying Qur’an, surahs, and righteous deeds as visible forms.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r2.claim: A second view weighs the record of deeds; the report of the card bearing There is no god but God outweighing ninety-nine scrolls is graded sound by al-Tirmidhi.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r3.claim: A third view weighs the person: a very heavy man may weigh less than a gnat’s wing, while Ibn Masud’s thin legs outweigh Mount Uhud.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389#2/r4.claim: Ibn Kathir sees no conflict: deeds, their records or forms, and the people who performed them may all be weighed at different times.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v3p389/r1.claim: The scales on Judgment Day weigh deeds with perfect justice; God wrongs no one, and the heavier scale brings success while the lighter one brings ruin.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r2.claim: The weighing may be of the records, the deeds after they are embodied in fitting forms, or another manner; God may simply give hearts knowledge of it.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r3.claim: Perhaps the weighing is attached to God's “We” in the preceding verse: He does not merely recount deeds but weighs them so everyone sees their exact equality.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r4.speaker: أبو حيان وعلي بن الحسن النحوي الأصفهاني
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r4.claim: They parse al-wazn as subject, yawma'idhin as its adverb, and al-haqq as predicate; al-Asbahani further objects that a definite verbal noun rarely governs, though 4:148 is an example.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r5.claim: The weighing is confined to truth: what occurs exactly matches it, with no excess or departure from the measure.

BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v3p9/r8.claim: Those with heavy scales are successful, attaining all their aims.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r1.claim: In a dialogue, the Prophet defines faith as belief in God, angels, books, messengers, Paradise and Hell, the balance, resurrection, and divine decree.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r10.claim: The balance has a tongue and two pans; heavy scales bring success, while light scales mean losing oneself and one's home in Paradise for wronging God's signs.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r2.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r2.claim: The weighing is justice; heavy scales mean good deeds, and the transmitted gloss for light scales also says good deeds.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن العيزار
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r3.claim: A caller beside the balance announces each person's lasting felicity or misery according to whether the scales are heavy or light.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r5.speaker: وهب بن منبه
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r5.claim: Only the endings of deeds are weighed: God grants a good ending to the one He wills good for and an evil ending to the one He wills evil for.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r6.speaker: الحارث الأعور
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r6.claim: Truth feels heavy to people of truth as it is heavy on the balance, and light to people of falsehood as it is light there.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r7.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r7.claim: Hasan says the balance has a tongue and two pans.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r8.speaker: كعب
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r8.claim: The balance is placed between two trees near Jerusalem.

DURR-FULL:v3p417/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r9.speaker: حذيفة
DURR-FULL:v3p417/r9.claim: Gabriel oversees the balances: an oppressor's good deeds are transferred to the victim, or the victim's sins to the oppressor if the oppressor has no good deeds.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r1.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r1.claim: Asked whether people remember their families at resurrection, the Prophet says not at the balance, when records fly, or at the bridge.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r2.claim: One more good deed than bad leads to Paradise and one more bad than good to Hell; equal deeds place a person among the people of the Heights, and a single grain can tip the balance.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r3.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r3.claim: A person whose outward state outweighs the inward has a light balance; one whose inward outweighs the outward has a heavy balance.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r4.speaker: جابر
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r4.claim: The Prophet says good and bad deeds are weighed; whichever side prevails determines entry to Paradise or Hell.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r5.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r5.claim: An angel announces a person's lasting felicity or misery according to whether the balance tips heavy or light.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r6.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r6.claim: The Prophet says people do not remember one another while the balance is placed, until each knows whether it is heavy or light.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r7.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r7.claim: The Prophet adds that people do not remember one another as records scatter until they know where each book lands, citing 69:19.

DURR-FULL:v3p418/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r8.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v3p418/r8.claim: At the bridge over Hell, hooks and thorns detain whom God wills until they know whether they will escape.

BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r1.claim: The weighing on that Day distinguishes deeds that are weighty or light, good or bad.

BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r2.claim: Heavy scales means the person's good deeds; mawāzīn may mean weighed things or balances, with the plural reflecting distinct objects or weighings.

BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r3.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r3.claim: The Najmī taʾwīl says every servant has several just balances suited to bodily attributes, spiritual qualities, secret states, and hidden ethics.

BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r4.speaker: النبي
BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r4.claim: The hidden spiritual faculty receives divine moral qualities; the Prophet says good character is the heaviest thing on the scale because people are commanded to emulate God's qualities.

BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p104#2/r5.claim: The plural ‘those’ follows the plural sense of ‘whoever,’ and the separate pronoun ‘they’ restricts the predicate to the successful.

BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v3p104#3/r1.claim: The successful are those who win salvation and reward.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r1.claim: The weighing is the weighing of deeds, distinguishing heavy from light and good from bad; the author parses 'the weight' as the subject, with 'on that day' as its predicate and 'true' as its description.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r10.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r10.claim: Another report from ʿAbd Allah b. ʿAmr depicts Adam watching descendants go to Paradise or Hell and Muhammad interceding for a member of his community with a tiny white card, identified as the sender's prayers upon the Prophet; it tips the scale and saves him.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r2.speaker: بعض المعربين
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r2.claim: Some grammarians instead make 'true' the predicate and 'on that day' the temporal modifier, avoiding a break between adjective and noun; the author notes that this uses a definite verbal noun in an uncommon way.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r3.speaker: الأصفهاني
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r3.claim: Al-Isfahani proposes that 'true' is an appositive to the implicit pronoun in the adverb, a sound parsing, though the author favors the first for meaning and the flexibility of adverbs.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r4.speaker: أبو البقاء
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r4.claim: Abu al-Baqa offers further parses in which either 'true' answers what the weighing is, or 'weight' is itself the predicate of an omitted subject; the author finds these strained.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r5.claim: A reading substitutes القسط, and al-Raghib defines weighing as determining a thing's measure, commonly with a balance or scales.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r6.speaker: الجمهور
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r6.claim: The majority, according to al-Qadi, hold that records of deeds are weighed on a balance with a tongue and two pans so people witness justice; the records' true nature is known to God.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r7.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r7.claim: A hadith describes a servant with ninety-nine enormous scrolls of sins, then a card bearing the two testimonies; it outweighs the scrolls, and nothing is heavier than God's name. Al-Hakim authenticated the report.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r8.speaker: القرطبي عن الحكيم الترمذي
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r8.claim: Al-Qurtubi, citing al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, says the card is not the basic testimony of monotheism, since scales set opposites against one another and one person cannot have both faith and disbelief; rather, the believer's later utterance is a good deed.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r9.speaker: غيره
ALUSI-FULL:v8p82#2/r9.claim: Others allow that the card is the testimony of monotheism, perhaps as a person's final words; they deny that the pans must contain opposites, so the impossibility objection does not follow.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r1.claim: If the report about the Prophet's intercession with the tiny card is sound, it magnifies his honored standing before God among all generations.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r2.claim: A hadith says a huge, heavy man will weigh no more than a mosquito's wing before God; the author questions how this view accounts for the other pan and notes that the report is not explicit proof that persons are weighed.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r3.claim: One view attributed to Ibn Abbas says deeds that appear as accidents in this world become fitting substances in the next; several authorities regard this as sound doctrine.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r4.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r4.claim: Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi reports that a person's deeds are placed in the scale, then cloud-like knowledge he taught people is placed in the other pan and tips it; Hammad b. Sulayman reports a similar account.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r5.speaker: مجاهد والأعمش والضحاك
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r5.claim: Mujahid, al-Aʿmash, and al-Dahhak, followed by the Muʿtazilites, take weighing as a metaphor for just judgment; some Muʿtazilites allow literal weighing rationally, while others deny it because deeds are nonenduring accidents, weighing has no benefit to an omniscient God, and useless action would be improper.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r6.speaker: الآمدي
ALUSI-FULL:v8p83/r6.claim: Al-Amidi objects that justice and fairness cannot be described as heavy or light; a report from Salman explicitly describes a corporeal scale vast enough for the heavens and Earth, which angels ask who could weigh.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p84#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84#2/r1.claim: The continuation identifies them as winners of salvation and reward, either with al-muflihun as predicate or as the predicate of a second subject; its definiteness marks the known or prototypical successful people of the Hereafter.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r1.speaker: عائشة
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r1.claim: Aisha reports that the two pans of the scale are as vast as the heavens and Earth; angels ask who will weigh with it, and God answers that He will weigh whoever He wills.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r2.speaker: داود
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r2.claim: A tradition says David saw the immense scale and fainted; God told him that if pleased with a servant He could fill a pan with half a date given in charity.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r3.speaker: الزجاج
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj says one should follow the transmitted hadiths about the scale because there is no reason to abandon them for figurative readings.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r4.speaker: بعض المحققين
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r4.claim: In response to the claim that believers already know God's justice and deniers will reject any scale, a scholar says weighing discloses the true realities and qualities of deeds, leaving no doubt that they are the same deeds performed in this world.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r5.claim: The plural 'balances' may refer to different weighings or weighed items, to an omitted word meaning pans, or to one scale for each deed.

ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v8p84/r6.claim: Those whose balances are heavy are successful: al-muflihun means those who attain salvation and reward; the plural points to the group, while pronoun and demonstrative forms track grammatical number and distance.

ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r7.claim: The weighing on that Day is real, fully just, and exact: unlike the partial accounting or respite before then, every deed and every balance of credit and debt will be measured and accounts closed.

ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r8.claim: The plural “scales” indicates that each individual has multiple scales, with the final result calculated from their combined total.

ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:7:1-9#2/r9.claim: Those whose good deeds, credits, and profits outweigh their sins, debts, and losses are the truly successful.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p27#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p27#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p27#2/r4.claim: The weighing follows the account of people's deeds: it manifests exact reward and punishment without injustice, except where God grants forgiveness or raises a rank.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r1.claim: The tanwin in يومئذ replaces an understood genitive: the day when people and messengers are questioned and their deeds recounted.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r2.claim: Here weighing means determining each deed's due reward or punishment precisely; a literal created scale that reveals deeds' measures is also possible.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r3.claim: The figurative measure varies with sincerity: a good deed for God differs from ostentation, as jihad for God's word differs from fighting for booty.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r4.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r4.claim: A report in the two Sahih collections says an enormous, heavy man will weigh no more than a mosquito's wing with God.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r5.speaker: الراعي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r5.claim: Al-Ra'i's verse uses weighing as a metaphor for considering and managing a matter.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r6.claim: The Prophet describes two expressions as light on the tongue but heavy in the balance, an example of the noun's figurative use.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r7.claim: Language about unseen events can only approximate their realities; verbal nouns without an instrument-taking verb are figurative, while noun forms may be literal or figurative and instrument-taking verbs imply a scale or analogy.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r8.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r8.claim: Reports cited from al-Tirmidhi mention the scale in the hadith of the testimony card and in the Prophet's instruction to Anas to seek him at the scale.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p28#2/r9.claim: No report describing the form of the scale is sound according to the author.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r1.claim: Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-A'mash deny a created scale and understand the weighing as just judgment; most early authorities affirm the literal scale.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r2.claim: Among later theologians, most Ash'arites and some Mu'tazilites affirm the scale, while some later Ash'arites and most Mu'tazilites follow the judgment interpretation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r3.claim: The author regards the disagreement as minor and the evidence as inconclusive: the intended meaning matters more than the instrument.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r4.claim: If weighing is metaphorical, الحق means just; if it depicts a scale, it means even and proportionate to deeds. Calling it by a verbal noun intensifies its reality.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r5.claim: The conditional clauses explain the weighing's outcome: success follows heavy measures and loss follows light ones.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r6.claim: Heavy measures metaphorically mean abundant, dominant good deeds; the weighed object is omitted because people ordinarily weigh prized goods whose exact amount matters.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p30#2/r8.claim: Success means obtaining good and attaining what one seeks.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r1.claim: The definite form of المفلحون may be generic or refer back to the established description in 2:5.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r2.claim: Although من is singular, it generically denotes everyone meeting the condition, allowing plural demonstrative and pronouns.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r3.claim: The demonstrative signals that their success results from heavy measures; its distance marks abstract, evaluative distance.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p31#2/r4.claim: The separating pronoun restricts realized success to this group alone.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v8p32#2/r3.claim: The passage addresses believers who all did good and polytheists devoid of good; mixed believers are outside its purpose and discussed elsewhere.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r1.claim: He concludes that deeds are weighed by truth: those containing the truth required in worship succeed, while works lacking it leave their owners ruined for denying God’s signs.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r2.claim: Judgment applies each deed to the truth proper to it; reward follows in proportion to that truth, and failure to contain it leads to ruin, so the verses can be read literally.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r3.claim: Another interpretation takes weighing as justice and heavy scales as predominance of good deeds, treating the language as metaphor.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#2/r4.claim: He rejects accounts that make the scales arbitrary and says each person has measures corresponding to the different truths in their deeds; the afterlife belongs wholly to truth and God.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r6.speaker: جابر
TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r6.claim: A report says good and evil deeds are weighed, and whichever side prevails determines entry into Paradise or Hell; the author accepts its content but not as an explanation of these verses.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r7.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
TABATABAI:7:1-9#3/r7.claim: Ali says a person whose outward appearance outweighs their inner state has a light scale, while inner reality outweighing outward appearance makes it heavy; the author says it does not explain the verses.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r1.speaker: عائشة
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r1.claim: A report says God fashioned the balance’s pans like heaven and earth and the path like a sword, saying he weighs and grants passage to whomever he wills.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r2.speaker: سلمان
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r2.claim: Al-Hakim reports a similar account from Salman.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r3.claim: He says these narrations depict an afterlife balance resembling the worldly instrument and are intended to make the idea accessible to unsophisticated hearers, as later reports clarify.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r4.speaker: هشام بن الحكم
TABATABAI:7:1-9#4/r4.claim: In a debate with a skeptic, Imam al-Sadiq says deeds are attributes rather than bodies, God does not need weighing to know their amount, and the balance means justice.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r1.claim: He explains deeds as moral qualities attached to actions, not the physical movements themselves: the same movement is lawful marriage or adultery according to its social or religious status.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r2.claim: The Imam’s argument has two parts: deeds as attributes have no physical weight, and God needs no weighing because nothing is hidden from him.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r3.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r3.claim: Some argue that embodied deeds can acquire weight, with the scale frightening sinners, encouraging the obedient, and displaying justice; they find problems in the Imam’s report.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r4.claim: He replies that deeds may appear embodied and justice may take the form of a balance; the report denies only worldly physical weight and does not require two-pan comparison.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r5.speaker: أمير المؤمنين عليه السلام
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r5.claim: A report says good deeds weigh down the balance while sins make it light; the author says this supports the truth in a deed as its measure.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r6.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r6.claim: Asked about the just balances, Imam al-Sadiq identifies them as the prophets and their successors.

TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9#5/r7.claim: He explains the report by saying prophets and Imams embody the measure of right action and belief.

TABATABAI:7:1-9/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r1.claim: The Quran’s ‘just balances’ means God’s just placement, not that the balance itself is justice; the wording ‘no soul is wronged’ shows that the justice belongs to God.

TABATABAI:7:1-9/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r2.claim: Commentators who take weighing as justice explain heaviness metaphorically as predominance of good deeds, and lightness as predominance of sins and loss of the self.

TABATABAI:7:1-9/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:1-9/r3.claim: That interpretation must still identify a just criterion for mixed, unequal good and bad deeds; otherwise the outcome would be arbitrary and would not complete the proof against people.

TABATABAI:7:7-8/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:7-8/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:7-8/r3.claim: The weighing concerns deeds, or people insofar as they acted; 21:47 places it within reckoning, while 99:7–8 explicitly assigns weight to good and evil deeds.

TABATABAI:7:7-8/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:7-8/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:7-8/r4.claim: Deeds erased through unbelief have no weight, so only deeds of those whose works are not nullified remain to be weighed.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r1.claim: He reads the weight as truth contained in deeds: good works have weight to the extent they embody truth, while evil is falsehood and has none.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r2.claim: The placed book identifies the truth in each deed and the weighing makes its amount manifest; he links this to judgment by truth and the book that speaks truth.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r3.claim: The plural ‘balances’ suits the distinct standards for different acts, since the truth of prayer differs from that of almsgiving, fasting, and pilgrimage.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r4.claim: Most commentators parse ‘the weighing is the truth’ as an initial subject with ‘the truth’ describing the weighing, meaning a just weighing; he considers another parsing possible but its reading of al-Kashshaf unusual.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#2/r5.claim: If ‘balances’ means weighed deeds, as some commentators suggest, their account still leaves unclear what determines relative heaviness when good and bad acts are mixed.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r1.speaker: علي بن الحسين عليه السلام
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r1.claim: Ali ibn al-Husayn says scales and records are set up for Muslims; polytheists are driven to Hell in groups, and he cites the verse about no weight for disbelievers.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r2.claim: He notes that the narration alludes to the statement that God will not assign the disbelievers any weight on Judgment Day.

TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9#3/r3.claim: Al-Qummi’s commentary interprets weighing as recompense according to deeds, good for good and evil for evil.

TABATABAI:7:8-9/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r1.claim: The verses portray good deeds as heavy and evil deeds as making the scales light, rather than weighing two piles and comparing their total mass.

TABATABAI:7:8-9/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r2.claim: Quranic parallels consistently place heaviness with good and lightness with evil, as in 23:102–103 and 101:6–10.

TABATABAI:7:8-9/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r3.claim: He proposes that each deed is tested by its own measure of truth: complete prayer, rightful almsgiving, and truthful speech exemplify standards that good deeds meet and sins fail.

TABATABAI:7:8-9/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:7:8-9/r4.claim: The comparison with a physical balance illustrates a single measure placed against the item; the measure itself determines whether the item has matching weight or is rejected.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r1.claim: Judgment aims to reward or punish justly according to the quantity and quality of deeds, which requires a measure; here ‘weight’ names that measure.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r2.speaker: İbn Âşûr
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r2.claim: Ibn Ashur reads ‘true’ as justice or equality: deeds are judged justly, with no injustice, or everyone receives an equivalent return.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r3.claim: Good deeds may receive more than their equivalent, bad deeds equivalent punishment, while repentance, intercession, or sheer divine mercy may forgive sins or increase rewards without violating justice.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r4.claim: Those whose scales are heavy, meaning their good deeds are more numerous, attain salvation.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r5.speaker: some commentators
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r5.claim: Some commentators say the things weighed are deeds made into tangible objects; others say they are the records of deeds.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r6.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r6.claim: Commentators differ over whether the weighing is a literal balance or metaphor; the manner and instrument are known to God.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:7:8/r7.claim: For people, the essential point is that God records intentions, thoughts, feelings, words, and actions, then counts and judges them completely fairly, rewarding or punishing by their nature and amount.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r1.claim: The weighing refers to each person's deeds being weighed and judgment rendered on the Last Day.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r10.claim: Together these themes suggest a universal cosmic balance that grounds equitable transactions and measures human acts for recompense in the next life.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r11.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r11.claim: Like the questioning in 7:6, weighing does not mean God needs an external source of information or judgment to know how people should be judged.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r12.speaker: Z
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r12.claim: The weighing rebukes wrongdoers by making them acknowledge their wrongdoing and abandon excuses.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r13.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r13.claim: The balance assures people that they have not been wronged because all deeds are judged by the same scale.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r2.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r2.claim: The weighing is true because it is just.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r3.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r3.claim: A heavy balance belongs to those with many good deeds or with good deeds outweighing bad ones.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r5.claim: A hadith says nothing is heavier in the balance than good character.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r6.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r6.claim: Another report indicates that belief in God’s oneness and Muhammad’s prophethood outweighs a vast record of sins.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r7.claim: The balance image is a metaphor for Divine Judgment and appears in other Qur’anic passages.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r8.claim: The judgment image accords with Qur’anic commands to weigh fairly and honestly in commercial dealings.

STUDYQURAN:7:8/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:7:8/r9.claim: The balance also fits the Qur’anic theme that creation is in due balance and that God sets the balance for the created order.
